source.title: In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in large language models
source.authors: Hua-Dong Xiong; Ji-An Li; Jiaqi Huang; Robert C. Wilson; Kwonjoon Lee; Xue-Xin Wei

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends superposition-like interference to online working-memory representations in LLMs, using behavioral, attention, representational, and intervention analyses rather than the original toy-model setup.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition but does not reproduce its sparse-feature toy-model method. It tests an in-context working-memory account; it does not test polysemantic neurons, SAE recovery or completeness, or whether LLM features are one-dimensional. The letter-direction suppression sweep selected and evaluated configurations on the same trials. Values stated only in plots are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows superposition from Elhage et al. (2022) as an analogy for in-context working-memory interference. Its results concern a different construct: overlap and interference among simultaneously active context items (N-back letters at different offsets) in LLM residual streams. It does not measure feature storage in toy networks, neuron polysemanticity or its causes, distribution of learned features across neurons, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. The authors say their use is geometric and does not establish a dimensional bottleneck. So no version is tested. The reader's 'tests'/T3 should be downgraded to discusses/T6, with the findings kept under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that LLM working-memory limits on N-back reflect interference among co-active context representations, which they call in-context superposition. They support this with recency and content biases, attention spread, overlapping positional representations, late target-readout alignment, and a sweep-identified intervention that helps. They also report that N-back accuracy correlates with MMLU Pro, GPQA and IFEval. They state that their use of superposition is geometric and does not establish a dimensional bottleneck.
record.recipe_differences: This is an inference-time N-back study in trained LLMs, using behavioral signatures, attention profiles, representational geometry, and residual-stream interventions. It does not use the original sparse-feature toy-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported interference patterns vary with memory load and evaluation mode; transition-structure effects differ between autoregressive generation and teacher forcing. The attention and intervention analyses use restricted model subsets.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM N-back performance declines with load. Retrieval is recency-biased and sensitive to lures, set size and transition statistics, and these sensitivities correlate with accuracy across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM N-back, concurrently active context items and stimulus statistics interfere with position-specified retrieval.

fits_no_version.finding: Target-selective heads in three models retain attention to recent non-target items. Relative-position representations separate in middle layers, then re-overlap late, with more overlap at higher N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representations of multiple in-context memory items remain geometrically overlapping ('in-context superposition') during retrieval.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual letter identity, positional similarity and target-readout alignment covary with recall (target alignment r ≈ .76–.78).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In N-back, layerwise interference-control geometry is associated with retrieval success.

fits_no_version.finding: Best-in-sweep suppression of letter-identity directions raised N-back accuracy in five models, more in weaker ones; no held-out test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing letter-identity residual directions can improve N-back retrieval under some configurations.

record.problems: The representational results are described by geometric similarities and do not establish a dimensional bottleneck; the authors say decomposition of item-position variables remains future work. The intervention reports best-in-sweep gains selected and evaluated on the same trials, so held-out generalization is untested. The strongest scaling comparisons are within the families studied, and the authors note possible instruction-following or prompt-format effects.

untested.parts: All: no toy model with sparse features exceeding dimensions, no sparsity transition, no geometry. The 2-layer transformer only shows N-back is solvable.
All: no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity competition among learned features.
All: polysemantic neurons and their alternative causes are not examined.
All: overlap is among offset-conditioned mean representations of context items, not learned features spread across neurons. No dictionary or SAE is used.
All: the authors explicitly leave decomposing item–position variables (and so dimensionality) to future work.

record.verdict_notes: Results not recorded as rows bear on no version: Table 3 benchmark correlations (e.g., GPQA r=.88 autoregressive) and the 2-layer transformer reaching 100% accuracy. 'Superposition' here names overlap among active context items, not learned-feature superposition in the Elhage sense, so the study should not count as evidence for or against V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse-feature toy networks with more features than dimensions, or their sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from feature competition for limited capacity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of neuron polysemanticity.
Measures in-context item representations, not feature distribution across neurons or sparse features recovered by a dictionary.
Does not test SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not establish whether the represented features are one-dimensional or multidimensional. The authors say that decomposing item-position variables is future work.

rows.subject: 10 trained LLMs (Gemma 3, Qwen 3.5, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Ministral 3 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured N-back accuracy under autoregressive generation as memory load increased.
rows.measure: Cohen's κ and accuracy
rows.value: Performance declined as N increased; most models approached chance by 3- or 4-back.
rows.note: Aggregate textual result across tested LLMs; model-specific raw accuracies are also reported in Appendix Table 4.

rows.subject: 10 trained LLMs (Gemma 3, Qwen 3.5, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Ministral 3 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured N-back accuracy with earlier answers teacher-forced to ground truth as memory load increased.
rows.measure: Cohen's κ and accuracy
rows.value: Performance remained higher than in autoregressive generation but still declined with N.
rows.note: Aggregate textual result; the paper states the qualitative decline persists when prior answers are correct.

rows.subject: 10 LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured probability mass assigned to the target and to recent non-target offsets.
rows.measure: Temporal retrieval-probability kernel and non-target recency mass
rows.baseline: Target offset is k = −N; non-target recent offsets are k = −N + 1 through 0.
rows.value: The kernel assigned disproportionate mass to recent non-target items, and this recency bias grew with memory load.
rows.uncertainty: ±1 SEM across models shown in the figure; numerical values not stated
rows.note: Text describes the pattern; plot values are not transcribed.

rows.subject: 10 LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related target retrieval probability to non-target recency interference across models.
rows.measure: Relationship between target retrieval probability and recency interference
rows.value: Higher target retrieval probability was associated with weaker recency interference.
rows.note: The relationship is described across models; a numerical correlation is not stated.
